summary: UC Merced — the newest campus in the entire University of California system, opened in 2005 — sits in a county that is otherwise almost entirely defined by agriculture, creating one of the stranger economic juxtapositions in the Central Valley: a research university rising from almond orchards and dairy operations on the flat, sun-drenched San Joaquin Valley floor. That flatness is absolute; the horizon stretches unbroken in most directions, though the Sierra Nevada foothills shimmer to the east, and Yosemite National Park is roughly 90 minutes up Highway 140. At a median home value of $368,400 against a median household income of $65,044, the price-to-income ratio lands near 5.7× — cheaper than coastal California but still a stretch that pushes many households toward renting at $1,284/month. The county functions partly as a bedroom community, with commuters heading north to Modesto or even making the grinding two-hour drive to Bay Area jobs, though agriculture, food processing, and the university anchor local employment. With nearly 1,978 square miles and just 150 people per square mile, the landscape between towns is open farmland under 9.7 hours of daily sunshine and summer highs that regularly push well past the 77°F annual average into triple digits. Merced is a place where the cost of entry is genuinely lower than most of California, but the tradeoff is distance from nearly everything that isn't sky, soil, or Sierra granite.
